findings.title: Statements that need a full lock should run with a lock timeout
findings.message: This migration locks 2 tables public.customers, public.orders against reads and writes. Each statement first waits for the queries already running there, and blocks all new ones while it waits.
findings.why: An ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock has to wait for every query already running on the table, even a slow report. While it waits, every new query on that table waits behind it. A statement that takes a millisecond can so stop an application for minutes.
findings.fix: Run SET lock_timeout = '5s' before the migration and try again if it times out. A failed attempt costs nothing; a waiting one blocks everybody.

findings.title: Column is dropped with all its values
findings.message: Dropping public.customers.name deletes its values in every row for good.
findings.why: DROP COLUMN makes the values of the column unreachable in every row, and they cannot be brought back without a backup. Application code that still selects or inserts the column fails at once, including code running during the deployment.
findings.fix: First release application code that no longer reads or writes the column, then drop it in a later migration. Keep a backup of the values until the change has proven itself.
findings.effect: DROP COLUMN takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on public.customers (blocks reads and writes), held briefly

findings.title: Possible rename would be applied as drop and add
findings.message: Column public.customers.name may have been renamed to full_name. Applied as drop and add, its values are lost.
findings.why: Two schemas alone cannot tell a rename from a drop followed by an add. The direct route does the second: it drops the old one and creates an empty new one, and the data is gone. If the intent was a rename, that is data loss nobody asked for. A real rename keeps the data, but it still breaks every query that uses the old name.
findings.fix: If it is a rename, write ALTER TABLE ... RENAME (TO or COLUMN) yourself. To rename without breaking the running application, add the new name next to the old one, write to both, move the readers over, and remove the old name last. If it is not a rename, nothing needs to change.
findings.change: ? column public.customers.name may have been renamed to full_name (confidence 0.86: same type and attributes; one name contains the other; both are column 3)

findings.title: Column type change rewrites the table
findings.message: Changing public.orders.id from integer to bigint rewrites the whole table while reads and writes wait.
findings.why: The stored bytes of the old type are not valid for the new one. PostgreSQL writes every row into a new copy of the table and rebuilds every index, all under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock: no reads, no writes, for as long as it takes. It also needs free disk space for the second copy.
findings.fix: Add a new column of the new type, fill it in batches, keep it in step with a trigger, then switch the application over and drop the old column. Some changes need no rewrite at all: a longer varchar, varchar to text, or a numeric with more digits and the same scale.
findings.effect: ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on public.orders (blocks reads and writes), held while the whole table is written again

findings.title: Foreign key is added without NOT VALID
findings.message: Adding foreign key orders_customer_id_fkey checks every row of public.orders against public.customers. Writes to both tables wait until the check ends.
findings.why: Adding a foreign key checks every existing row against the referenced table. For the whole check it holds a SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE lock on both tables, which blocks all writes to them. It also fails if one row points to a row that does not exist.
findings.fix: Add the constraint with NOT VALID: it then applies to new rows only and is quick. Run ALTER TABLE ... VALIDATE CONSTRAINT as a second statement; it checks the existing rows without blocking reads or writes.
findings.effect: ADD CONSTRAINT ... FOREIGN KEY takes SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE on public.orders (blocks writes, reads continue) and SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE on public.customers (blocks writes, reads continue), held while every row is read
findings.change: + constraint public.orders.orders_customer_id_fkey FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES public.customers (id)

findings.title: Index is built without CONCURRENTLY
findings.message: Building index orders_status_idx blocks every write to public.orders until the build ends.
findings.why: CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock on the table for the whole build. Reads continue, but every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE waits, and on a large table the build takes minutes or hours.
findings.fix: Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. It builds the index without blocking writes. It cannot run inside a transaction, and if it fails it leaves an invalid index that has to be dropped before trying again. With Flyway, set postgresql.transactional.lock=false and connect directly, not through a transaction pooler: under Flyway's default lock the build waits forever for Flyway's own open transaction.
findings.effect: CREATE INDEX takes SHARE on public.orders (blocks writes, reads continue), held while every row is read
findings.change: + index public.orders_status_idx ON public.orders USING btree (status)
